newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN RECOVERY HINGES ON RADICAL REFORM.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN RECOVERY HINGES ON RADICAL REFORM.

text.p: Bulgaria's ambitious reform plan will be difficult to sustain unless its key elements -- speedy sell-offs, stabilising banks and curbing tax evasion -- are implemented at the same time, analysts say.

"The problem is that all these, restoring confidence in the currency and the banks, servicing domestic and foreign debts, tax reform and reducing the deficit need to be done at the same time," said Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics.
"And it would not be difficult for those who want to make the reform fail to do so," Stanchev told Reuters.
Bulgaria has agreed a package of credits worth nearly $1.2 billion with the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the European Union and the G-24 industrialised countries.
The $657 million IMF accord paves the way for negotiations with the Paris Club on a rescheduling of foreign debt payments which total $1 billion this year.
As a condition of the IMF accord, Bulgaria has pledged to introduce a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime in June to restore confidence in the economy.
Central bank lending to the budget and commercial banks will be banned under the currency board system. Privatisation proceeds and taxes will be the only source of budget revenue.

Bulgaria's foreign and domestic debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio is estimated at between 180 and 300 percent depending on the calculation method, according to the Economy Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS).
"Sustaining both debt payments and reducing budget spending to a 3.8 percent deficit will be very difficult," said BAS expert Garabed Minasian.
The IMF agreement envisages bringing down the budget deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP from last year's 12 percent.
Bulgaria expects some $300 million from privatisation of major state owned firms this year, but a major sell-offs have yet to be completed.
Economic Policy Minister Krassimir Angarski has called for urgent revision of tax laws to boost budget revenue. Businesses avoiding taxes account for 50 percent of GDP, according to BAS.

Asset stripping of state enterprises by a small group of private firms is seen as one of the causes of Bulgaria's grave economic crisis. Analysts warn corrupt business interests still could thwart radical reform plans.
Stabilising the country's troubled banks and guaranteeing deposits in closed banks will also require funds. The currency board removes the central bank's role as lender of last resort.
"No insolvent or illiquid banks should enter the currency board system," said Angarski.

Bulgaria hopes to sell majority stakes in six big state banks by mid-1998. The state of the six -- Bulbank, Post Bank, Biochimbank, United Bulgarian Bank, Hebrosank, Expressbank -- has improved recently after the lev's drastic slump in February because these banks held long positions in foreign exchange.
The remaining eight private banks, which share three percent of the local market, will need to find a particular market niche, otherwise they risk bankruptcy, said Stanchev.

The Bank Consolidation Company is drafting procedures for bank sales either through tenders or with direct talks with investors. The procedure has yet to be approved by the new government to be formed after April 19 elections.

Of Bulgaria's 45 banks, four have been declared insolvent by the courts -- Crystalbank, Mineralbank, Private Agricultural Investment Bank and Trade and Savings Bank. A further 12 were placed in receivership.

The IMF and the cabinet have prepared a revision of the bank insolvency law that will allow the swift resolution of pending court cases and speed up liquidation of closed banks. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-91188
